Corrective review of the belt id index; supersedes this branch's earlier entry for the same sources, which recorded two claims that were false. The index now cannot disagree with the belt: RoidBelt owns every membership change, `roids` is private, readers take a readonly view through getRoids(), and the Map is maintained by add(), remove() and replaceAll() rather than rebuilt when the array looks different. Nothing watches the array any more, so there is no invalidation heuristic to get wrong.

Why it changed. The earlier revision rebuilt the index whenever the public array's identity or length stopped matching what was indexed. That cannot see a removal and an addition that net to the same length on the same array object, and both production mutators worked that array in place. The pairing is ordinary traffic rather than a contrived order: applyAsteroidFieldPartition fans created before updated before removed, and every complete snapshot populates removed for rocks leaving WORLD.asteroidInterestRadius, so one rock arriving as one leaves holds the length at the indexed value across both lookups. The index then kept the departed rock and never saw the arrival.

That was player-visible, which is why the earlier entry is superseded rather than merely extended. applyServerAsteroidUpdated silently applied no kinematics to the arriving rock, so it sat where the snapshot first placed it. removeServerAsteroid returned early for it, so its asteroidDestroy event dropped playDestructionSound and recordAsteroidShatter and left the rock rendered in the belt. A twelve-tick one-in, one-out run reproduced ten missed updates and two missed reconciliations. The earlier entry said "the destroy path still plays the same sound and records the same shatter for the same rock object" and "the guard covers every way callers edit the array behind the index". Both were false on that path. Its mutation check used a build-once index that never invalidates, which is a strictly weaker defect than the real one -- a never-invalidating index strands a spliced rock immediately, so the weaker mutation failed the old guard while the real defect passed it. The replacement guard is mutation-checked by restoring the identity-and-length heuristic itself, which fails both of its new cases with the arriving rock unfindable.
